blocks.content: Is your site up right now? Synthetic Monitoring answers that continuously. Probes around the world test your target on a schedule, from outside your network, whether or not your browser is open. You'll create the simplest kind: a ping check.
First, open Synthetic Monitoring:
Click **Testing & synthetics** in the main menu.
Click **Synthetics**.

whenTrue.content: Click **Get started** to set up Synthetic Monitoring in your stack. First-time setup needs the **Admin** role.

blocks.content: Once Synthetic Monitoring is open, you're ready to create a check.
You need the **Editor** or **Admin** role.
Click **Create new check**.
Click **API Endpoint**. Ping lives here, alongside HTTP, DNS, and TCP checks.
Name the check so you can find it again later, for example `my-first-uptime-check`.
Under **Request type**, click **Ping** to send a network packet and wait for a response.
Enter the hostname to check: your own site, or `grafana.com` to try it out.
In the numbered bar at the top, click **Execution** (step 4) to choose where the check runs from.
Select one or more probe locations. Pick places near your users, plus one far away to see the difference distance makes.
Click **Save**. The check starts running on its schedule (every minute by default) and its dashboard opens.
Your check is live. Probes are already pinging the target from the locations you picked.
Finally, read the results on the dashboard that just opened:
**Uptime** is the percentage of checks that succeeded. Give it a few minutes to populate, and refresh if it's empty.
**Reachability** shows how often the target responds, per probe location.
**Average latency** shows how long the response takes from each location. Distance shows up here.
You have continuous, outside-in monitoring of your site, and it keeps running after you close this browser.

One habit worth starting now: each probe runs the check separately, so a check's usage is its frequency multiplied by its probe count. A check that runs every minute from five probes costs five times the executions of the same check from one probe. Give each check the frequency and probe count its target actually needs, not the maximum.
